intro: How much income Australian residents can earn before paying income tax, how to claim the threshold from an employer, and how it works for part of a year.
explanation:
## Only Australian residents for tax purposes can claim it

The tax-free threshold is available to people who are Australian residents for tax purposes. A person who is a non-resident for the whole year cannot claim it and is taxed on all of their Australian income. If you are a resident for only part of the year, a smaller threshold applies in place of the full amount. Residency for tax purposes is a separate test from immigration status.

## Claiming it reduces the tax withheld from your pay

When you start with a payer, you complete a **tax file number (TFN) declaration**, and that form is where you say whether to claim the threshold. A payer can be an employer or a government agency such as Centrelink. If you choose not to claim it, more tax is withheld, and any excess may come back as a refund when you lodge your tax return.

The threshold applies to your income across an **income year**, the period from the start of July to the end of the following June.

## With more than one payer, the choice depends on your total income

If you have more than one payer, how much tax is withheld depends on which payers you claim the threshold from. If you are certain your total income from all payers will be {fact:au_tax_free_threshold} or less, you can choose to claim it from each payer. Otherwise, claiming it from more than one payer can leave too little tax withheld, and you may receive a tax bill when you lodge.
meta_description: Australian residents can earn {fact:au_tax_free_threshold} a year before income tax applies. How to claim it from an employer and how part-year residents are treated.

intro: What the Medicare levy is and who pays it, how reductions and exemptions work, and how the levy differs from the separate Medicare levy surcharge.
explanation:
## The levy is a percentage of your taxable income

Medicare, the public health system, is partly paid for by the Medicare levy. You pay it on top of income tax, at {fact:au_medicare_levy_rate} of your **taxable income**, which is your assessable income minus any allowable deductions.

The ATO calculates the amount once you lodge your return. Tax withheld from your pay by your employer generally covers part of it.

## Reductions and exemptions are considered separately

Depending on your income, your spouse's income and your circumstances, you may pay a reduced levy or none at all. Qualifying for a reduction and qualifying for an exemption are separate questions, so one does not settle the other.

## The Medicare levy surcharge is a different charge

On top of the levy, some people owe a surcharge of their own, called the **Medicare levy surcharge** (MLS). Whether you owe it depends on your personal circumstances.
meta_description: The Medicare levy is {fact:au_medicare_levy_rate} of taxable income, paid on top of income tax. Who pays it, who can get a reduction or exemption and how the surcharge differs.

intro: The income tax rates for Australian residents, the income thresholds where each rate starts, and what the rates leave out, including the Medicare levy.
explanation:
## Each rate applies only to the income inside its band

The ATO sets out each band as an amount of tax plus a number of cents for every dollar above the band's starting point. A rate therefore applies only to the part of your **taxable income** that sits inside its band. Crossing into a higher band does not raise the tax on the income below it. The bands are measured on taxable income, so allowable deductions come off before any rate is applied.

## These rates assume a full-year resident with the full tax-free threshold

Someone who was a tax resident all year and gets the whole {fact:au_tax_free_threshold} tax-free threshold can use these rates. Part-year residents and non-residents are treated differently, as the [tax-free threshold](/au/tax/income-tax/tax-free-threshold/) page explains.

## The Medicare levy is charged on top of these rates

Both the Medicare levy ({fact:au_medicare_levy_rate} of taxable income) and the separate Medicare levy surcharge are charged in addition to the tax these rates produce. The [Medicare levy](/au/tax/income-tax/medicare-levy/) page covers the levy and how it differs from the surcharge.
meta_description: Australian resident income tax rates for {tax_year}, from {fact:au_tax_rate_band_1} to {fact:au_tax_rate_top}, with the taxable income where each rate starts and what the rates leave out.

intro: The National Minimum Wage for employees who are not covered by an award or agreement, what it is per hour and per week, and when each increase starts.
explanation:
## The National Minimum Wage applies when no award or agreement does

Awards decide the minimum wage for most employees, though every employee in Australia is entitled to one. The National Minimum Wage, {fact:au_min_wage_hourly} an hour or {fact:au_min_wage_weekly} a week, is the rate for employees who are covered by neither an award nor a registered agreement. Its legal basis is the Fair Work Act 2009.

## An award or agreement sets the rate instead

Where an award or registered agreement covers an employee, the pay it sets applies in place of the national rate, and it may be higher. Awards and registered agreements also set penalty rates and allowances. Some awards pay employees an introductory rate when they start in an industry, for a limited time, and that rate can be lower than the national rate.

## The rate is reviewed each year and changes usually start in July

Every year the Fair Work Commission carries out an annual wage review of the national rate and of award rates. Any change usually takes effect with the first full pay period that begins from the start of July.
meta_description: The National Minimum Wage is {fact:au_min_wage_hourly} an hour or {fact:au_min_wage_weekly} a week for a full-time employee. Who it covers and when each yearly increase takes effect.

intro: How much Age Pension a single person or a couple can get, what the rate is made up of, who is eligible and how income and assets change the amount.
explanation:
## The figures are maximum rates made up of three parts

The cards show the most a person can be paid each fortnight, before tax. Each total adds together a basic rate, the **Pension Supplement** and the **Energy Supplement**. A couple living apart because of ill health is paid the single rate, not the couple rate.

## Reaching Age Pension age is only the first condition

The age requirement is {fact:au_age_pension_age}, with no change planned. Reaching that age is not enough on its own, because residence, income and assets are also tested. An ophthalmologist's report can support a claim by a legally blind person who is not claiming Rent Assistance, and the income and assets tests may then not be applied. Whether a person qualifies can also depend on any payments they get from the Department of Veterans' Affairs. People of that age who miss out on the pension may be eligible instead for a Commonwealth Seniors Health Card, which can cut the cost of medicines.

## Income and assets decide how much you are paid

The income test can reduce the payment, and the assets test affects both whether you are paid and how much. For someone with a partner, the income and assets of both partners are needed, and a change in the relationship can change the rate. Any work income of yours or your partner's has to be reported, including amounts below the income cut off point. Income or assets held outside Australia can also affect the payment.

## Some people are paid a transitional rate

People who were already on a part pension in September 2009 may be paid a transitional rate, which was set for pensioners who would otherwise be paid less, until the normal rates catch up. The cards show the normal rates, not these.

## Age Pension is taxable

The payment is taxable, but no tax is deducted unless you ask for it, and asking can prevent a bill when you lodge your return.
meta_description: The maximum Age Pension is {fact:au_age_pension_single} a fortnight for a single person and {fact:au_age_pension_couple_each} each for a couple. How the rate is made up and who qualifies.

intro: How much you can put into super each year at the concessional and non-concessional rates, which contributions count towards each cap, and what happens if you go over.
explanation:
## Each cap counts what you put in across all your funds

Which cap a contribution uses depends on its type. Employer payments, including salary sacrifice, and personal payments that you claim as a tax deduction are concessional. Personal payments that you don't claim, or can't claim, are non-concessional.

Concessional contributions to every fund you hold are added together and measured against the concessional cap, and non-concessional contributions are added together and measured against the non-concessional cap. Spreading money over several funds does not create extra room under either cap.

## A large balance can reduce the non-concessional cap to nil

If your total super balance at the end of the previous financial year reached the general transfer balance cap ({fact:au_transfer_balance_cap}), the non-concessional cap for the next year is nil. Any non-concessional contribution you make in that year counts as excess.

Some people below a set age limit can also use the bring-forward option and put in up to three times the annual cap in one year. Going over the annual cap triggers it automatically and unlocks the caps of the following years. How much you can bring forward, and for how many years, depends on your balance just before the year starts.

## Unused concessional cap can be carried forward, but it expires

If your total super balance was under {fact:au_carry_forward_balance_limit} on 30 June of the previous financial year, you can use cap you left unused in earlier years to contribute more than the general concessional cap in a year.

Each year's unused amount stays available for {fact:au_carry_forward_years}. Whatever is still unused when that time is up is lost.

## Excess contributions are taxed differently for each cap

Concessional contributions above your cap are added to your taxable income and taxed at your marginal rate. The extra excess concessional contributions charge no longer applies to contributions made from 1 July 2021.

For excess non-concessional contributions, you can choose to have the excess released from super. The ATO then works out an associated earnings amount, an estimate of what the excess earned while it was in the fund, and adds it to your assessable income.

## The CGT cap is a separate lifetime limit

Money from selling certain small business assets can be left out of the non-concessional cap, up to the capital gains tax (CGT) cap. It is a limit over your lifetime, not one that resets each year.
meta_description: Super contribution caps: {fact:au_concessional_cap} concessional and {fact:au_non_concessional_cap} non-concessional. See carry-forward rules, balance limits and excess contributions.

intro: A business must register for GST when its turnover reaches {fact:au_gst_threshold}, or {fact:au_gst_threshold_nonprofit} for a non-profit. Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must always register.
explanation:
## GST turnover is business income, not profit

The threshold is tested against your GST turnover. That is your total business income rather than your profit, less a few amounts:

- the GST that is already part of your sales
- sales to associates that are neither paid for nor taxable
- sales made outside the enterprise you run
- input-taxed sales
- sales not connected with Australia

## Two tests decide whether you have reached the threshold

You reach the threshold if either test is met. The first looks back: your turnover for the current month and the months before it that make up a full year is at or above {fact:au_gst_threshold}. The second looks ahead: your turnover for the current month and the months still to come that make up a full year is likely to be at or above that amount. A non-profit organisation uses {fact:au_gst_threshold_nonprofit} for both tests.

When you estimate the forward-looking figure, leave out money from selling a business asset such as a capital asset, any sale you make only because you are closing the enterprise, and sales you will lose by shrinking it substantially and permanently. Even if the backward-looking figure is at or above the threshold, you can stay unregistered if the ATO accepts that your projected turnover will fall short.

## You have {fact:au_gst_register_days} to register once you are required

A new business that expects to reach the threshold during its first year must register. Everyone else should check each month whether they have reached it or are likely to. Once registration is required, you have {fact:au_gst_register_days} to complete it.

You need an Australian business number (ABN) first, and you register once however many businesses you run. Registration can be done online, by phoning the ATO's Business enquiries line, or through your tax agent or BAS agent. Once registered, you start lodging business activity statements.

## Some businesses must register whatever their turnover

Anyone providing taxi or limousine travel, ride-sourcing included, has to register regardless of turnover, whether they own the vehicle or lease or rent it. Wanting to claim fuel tax credits for a business also means registering. For everyone else registration is optional, but if you choose it you are generally committed for at least {fact:au_gst_min_registration_months}.

## Registering late can be costly

If you were required to register and did not, you may be liable for GST on the sales you made from the date you should have registered, even where you never added GST to your prices. Penalties and interest can apply as well.

You can ask for your registration to be backdated, but no further than {fact:au_gst_backdate_years} back, unless fraud or evasion is involved. Requests are made by phoning Business enquiries.

## GST groups and branches

Related entities can form a single GST group, and an entity may register a branch separately where that suits how it is managed and accounted for. If you belong to a group, the other members' turnover counts towards yours, while dealings between members are ignored.
meta_description: When a business must register for GST in Australia: the {fact:au_gst_threshold} turnover threshold, {fact:au_gst_threshold_nonprofit} for non-profits, and how long you have to register.

intro: Employers must pay super of at least {fact:au_super_guarantee_rate} of qualifying earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of {fact:au_super_max_contribution_base} a year in {tax_year}.
explanation:
## The minimum is a percentage of each employee's earnings

The super guarantee is the least an employer must pay into an eligible employee's super. The rate is {fact:au_super_guarantee_rate}. It reached this level on 1 July 2025 after rising in steps over several years, and the ATO's table shows it staying there in the years after.

From 1 July 2026 the percentage is applied to an employee's qualifying earnings. For quarters up to the end of June 2026 it was applied to ordinary time earnings.

## Payday Super changes when employers pay

Payday Super starts on 1 July 2026 and ties each super payment to the day an employee is paid. Before then, contributions for each employee were due at least once a quarter, so payments now follow every pay run instead of a quarterly cycle.

## There is a ceiling on the earnings it applies to

The maximum contribution base limits the earnings on which an employer has to pay the minimum. For {tax_year} it is {fact:au_super_max_contribution_base} a year. Employers do not have to pay super guarantee on earnings above it. Once an employee's qualifying earnings reach the base in a financial year, the employer can stop paying the minimum for that employee until the next financial year starts.

## The base is worked out from the concessional contributions cap

The ATO calculates the base from the concessional contributions cap and the super guarantee percentage, then rounds the result down to a whole multiple of ten dollars. The base also rises over time with average weekly ordinary time earnings, a measure produced by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

## Earlier years used a quarterly base

For quarters up to the end of June 2026, the base was an amount of earnings per quarter, with a matching maximum super guarantee payment for each quarter. Because the basis changed, figures for earlier years are not directly comparable with the annual base.
meta_description: Australia's super guarantee rate is {fact:au_super_guarantee_rate} of qualifying earnings, with a maximum contribution base of {fact:au_super_max_contribution_base} for {tax_year}. Paid every payday.

intro: The age you must reach before you can access your super, set by your date of birth. For anyone born from 1 July 1964 it is {fact:au_preservation_age_from_1964}.
meta_description: Australia's preservation age by date of birth: {fact:au_preservation_age_pre_1960} if born before 1 July 1960, rising to {fact:au_preservation_age_from_1964} from 1 July 1964. See the full table.

intro: JobSeeker Payment is paid every two weeks, and the most you can get depends on your circumstances. A single person with no children can get up to {fact:au_jobseeker_single}.
explanation:
## Who can get JobSeeker Payment

JobSeeker Payment is income support for people who are out of work or temporarily unable to work. To qualify you must be aged from {fact:au_jobseeker_min_age} up to Age Pension age, which is {fact:au_age_pension_age}, meet the residence rules and pass the income and assets tests. You must also either be without a job and looking for one, or be unwell or injured so that you cannot do your normal work or study for a short period.

You do not have to be out of work completely. People in part-time or casual work, people who have been stood down and people whose hours have been cut can qualify too.

## How much you can get

Services Australia pays JobSeeker every two weeks, and the amount depends on your circumstances. These are the maximums:

- Single, with no children: {fact:au_jobseeker_single}
- Single with one or more dependent children: {fact:au_jobseeker_single_child}
- Partnered: {fact:au_jobseeker_partnered}
- Single principal carer with an exemption from mutual obligation requirements, for reasons such as foster caring or home schooling: {fact:au_jobseeker_carer_exempt}

The rate for a single person with children also applies in a couple of other situations, which Services Australia lists in its rates table. These are maximums. How much you are paid depends on the income that you and your partner have received in the past fortnight, and the income and assets tests can reduce it.

## Rates are updated twice a year

Services Australia updates the rates on 20 March and 20 September each year, so the amounts above change at those dates. Its own table is a guide only, and the payment finder gives an estimate for your situation.

## Children and child support

While you have a dependent child, the higher single rate applies, and in some cases it can continue as the child gets older. You need to tell Services Australia about any change in your circumstances. JobSeeker can also have an effect on child support, whether you pay it or receive it.

## Tax on the payment

JobSeeker Payment is a taxable Centrelink payment. If you ask Services Australia to, tax can be taken out of each payment, which may lower what you owe when you lodge your return.
meta_description: JobSeeker Payment maximum rates in Australia: {fact:au_jobseeker_single} for a single person with no children and {fact:au_jobseeker_partnered} for a partnered person, every fortnight.

intro: Employees covered by the National Employment Standards get {fact:au_annual_leave_weeks} of paid annual leave a year, and some shiftworkers get {fact:au_annual_leave_shift_extra} more.
explanation:
## What the National Employment Standards give you

Paid annual leave is one of the minimum entitlements in the National Employment Standards. The minimum is {fact:au_annual_leave_weeks} of paid leave each year, and some shiftworkers receive {fact:au_annual_leave_shift_extra} more.

## Who it applies to

The standards apply to employees in the national workplace relations system, which takes in most Australian employers and their staff, with a few exclusions. Casual employees get only some of the entitlements, and annual leave is not one the Fair Work Ombudsman lists for them.

## Awards and agreements can add to it

An award, enterprise agreement or employment contract cannot give you less than the standards, and a term that does has no effect. These documents can deal with practical matters, such as how annual leave is cashed out and taken, and they can offer more favourable terms than the minimum.

For the detail on how leave builds up and how it is taken, the Fair Work Ombudsman has a separate annual leave fact sheet.
meta_description: How much paid annual leave employees get in Australia under the National Employment Standards: {fact:au_annual_leave_weeks} a year, plus {fact:au_annual_leave_shift_extra} more for some shiftworkers.

intro: Employees get {fact:au_sick_leave_days} of paid sick and carer's leave under the National Employment Standards, plus unpaid carer's leave, compassionate leave and paid family and domestic violence leave.
explanation:
## Paid leave for sickness and caring

An employee covered by the National Employment Standards gets {fact:au_sick_leave_days} of paid sick and carer's leave, reduced in proportion for part-time staff. Paid sick and carer's leave is not on the Fair Work Ombudsman's list of entitlements that reach casual employees.

## Unpaid carer's leave and compassionate leave

Employees can take up to {fact:au_unpaid_carers_days} of unpaid carer's leave when it is needed, and up to {fact:au_compassionate_days} of compassionate leave when it is needed. Casual employees can take both, unpaid, for each occasion.

## Family and domestic violence leave

Paid family and domestic violence leave is a yearly entitlement of {fact:au_fdv_leave_days}. Casual employees have it too, measured across a year.

## Awards and agreements can add to it

An award, agreement or contract has to meet the standards, and any term that falls short has no effect. These documents may deal with cashing out paid sick and carer's leave, and may offer extra sick and carer's leave or annual leave if the employee gives up the same value in pay.
meta_description: Paid sick and carer's leave in Australia: {fact:au_sick_leave_days}, plus unpaid carer's leave, compassionate leave and {fact:au_fdv_leave_days} of paid family and domestic violence leave.

intro: Parental Leave Pay is paid at {fact:au_ppl_daily_rate} a day before tax, with {fact:au_ppl_days} available to a family for a child born or adopted from 1 July 2026.
explanation:
## What the payment is

Parental Leave Pay is a taxable payment for parents of a new or newly adopted child, and it is based on the national minimum wage. Your employer often delivers it to you, and sometimes Services Australia pays you directly. With a multiple birth, such as twins, it is paid for only one child.

## How much it pays

The payment is worked out for each day, and the daily amount before tax is {fact:au_ppl_daily_rate}. For a five day week that comes to {fact:au_ppl_weekly_rate}. Expect the rate to be revised at the start of each financial year.

The rate depends on the financial year in which you take your leave, and not on when your child was born or adopted. If your days fall in two financial years, you can be paid at two different rates.

## How many days a family can get

The number of days depends on the child's date of birth or adoption, and it has gone up in steps on 1 July. For a child born or adopted from 1 July 2026, a family can get {fact:au_ppl_days}. If you claim before the birth and the child arrives before that date, your balance starts at the earlier, lower number. Once Services Australia has proof of the birth or adoption, the extra days are added without a new claim.

## Sharing days between parents

A single parent gets all of the days, and can approve sharing them with another parent. With a partner, part of the entitlement is set aside for them, and the two of you agree how the remainder is used. For a child born or adopted from 1 July 2026, {fact:au_ppl_reserved_days} are reserved for the partner.

There is also a cap on how many days can be taken at the same time. For a child born or adopted from 1 July 2025 it is {fact:au_ppl_concurrent_days}, and some exemptions apply.

## Super on top of the payment

Where the child was born or adopted on or after 1 July 2025, the ATO adds a contribution to your super, known as the Paid Parental Leave Superannuation Contribution. It is based on the super guarantee rate, which is {fact:au_super_guarantee_rate}. The ATO calculates it and pays it into your super fund after the financial year ends, so there is nothing extra to claim.
meta_description: Parental Leave Pay in Australia: {fact:au_ppl_daily_rate} a day before tax, up to {fact:au_ppl_days} for a family, with {fact:au_ppl_reserved_days} reserved for a partner. See how super is added.
